c.v: Does chimney flashing go over or under shingles?

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to repair chimney flashing in Montclair?

runs.v: A repair of the roof covering, including chimney flashing, on a detached one- or two-family home counts as ordinary maintenance under N.J.A.C. 5:23-2.7 and needs no construction permit, per the NJ Uniform Construction Code; on a commercial, multi-family, or attached building, a permit is typically required once repairs exceed 25% of the roof area in 12 months. A historic-district or landmark property can need extra review, so confirm with the Montclair construction office before work; per the National Park Service, National Register listing alone places no federal restriction on a private owner.

faqs.q: Why does chimney flashing leak more than the rest of the roof?

runs.v: On Montclair's grand period homes the chimney is the roof's largest penetration, and the apron, the sidewall step runs, and the upslope head all share that one masonry transition, so a single failed counter flashing or cracked caulk joint admits water into the chase. Water intrusion often occurs through poorly installed or corroded chimney flashing, and common flashing issues include corroded metal and deteriorated sealant.

faqs.q: Is caulk a permanent fix for chimney flashing on a Montclair home?

runs.v: No. On the century-old masonry chimneys common across Montclair, caulk or roofing cement alone over no underlying metal cracks within a few years, per IIBEC, so decline a door-to-door offer to tar the joint. To fix damaged flashing around a chimney, lift the surrounding shingles, replace the step flashing piece by piece, and reset the counter flashing into a reglet cut in the mortar joint.

faqs.q: Does my Montclair chimney need a cricket?

runs.v: A Montclair chimney wider than 30 inches measured parallel to the ridge takes a cricket, or saddle, on its upslope side, per IRC Section R1003.20. The cricket sheds water, ice, and snow around the masonry rather than letting the upslope face dam the leaf and branch debris that the township's mature street-tree canopy drops against it.
